power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: The visual evoked potential (VEP) indexes sensory processing, but the neurophysiological basis of altered VEP amplitudes in autism remains unclear.

We examined whether reduced VEP amplitude reflects increased trial-to-trial neural variability and whether this variability relates to electrophysiological markers of cortical excitation/inhibition and developmental functioning.
Pattern-reversal VEPs were analyzed in 102 typically developing (TD; 44 female) and 105 autistic (AUT; 15 female) children aged 2-12 years.
N1 and N1-P1 amplitudes and inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC) were computed.
Resting-state periodic alpha activity and aperiodic exponent were derived using spectral parameterization.
Associations among VEP, resting EEG, age, and developmental/behavioral measures were assessed using multiple linear regression.
AUT children exhibited reduced N1 amplitude and lower ITPC, with marginally reduced N1-P1 amplitude.
Higher ITPC was strongly associated with larger N1 and N1-P1 amplitudes, and group differences in VEP amplitudes were no longer significant after accounting for ITPC.
Greater periodic alpha activity was associated with higher ITPC and larger N1-P1 amplitude, while a steeper aperiodic exponent was associated with higher ITPC in the pooled cohort.
Within AUT children, higher ITPC was associated with better nonverbal development, verbal cognition, and language scores.
Reduced VEP amplitudes in autism may primarily reflect increased trial-to-trial variability rather than systematically weaker stimulus-evoked responses.
Associations between ITPC and resting EEG measures suggest that cortical excitation/inhibition may contribute to sensory response reliability.
These findings identify neural response consistency as a developmentally relevant feature of visual processing in autism.

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition defined by deficits in social communication and restricted or repetitive behaviors and interests (Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders: DSM-5., 2013), with marked heterogeneity in presentations and symptoms across individuals (Amaral et al., 2008; Baiano & Zeppieri, 2023; Halder et al., 2024).

text.text: Indeed, dysregulation in sensory processing is hypothesized to contribute to social symptoms of autism (Markram & Markram, 2010; Thye et al., 2018), as altered processing of and responsiveness to one's external environment may affect social responsiveness.

text.text: Understanding the neural underpinnings of sensory atypicalities in autism may therefore shed light on the developmental pathways contributing to social and behavioral differences and can help identify brain-based markers associated with heterogeneity in this population.

Neuroimaging tools and experimental paradigms have been developed to characterize neural responses to sensory input in autism, among which the visual evoked potential (VEP) has emerged as a promising approach.

Using electroencephalography (EEG) and simple visual stimuli, the VEP paradigm was originally developed to investigate the function of the visual pathway from the optic nerve to the visual cortex (Shigihara et al., 2016; Šuštar Habjan et al., 2025).

text.text: VEPs are typically studied by averaging the evoked response across trials and examining components such as the N1 and P1, which are extracted from the average waveform.
The amplitude and latency of these components provide information about neural responses and timing of information transmission through the visual system (Baiano & Zeppieri, 2023; Creel, 2019).

text.text: In neurotypical adults, VEP measures have shown high reliability across and within sessions (Tello et al., 2010; Trevino et al., 2018).

text.text: More recently, VEPs have become an increasingly utilized tool for studying atypical visual system development in young children with neurodevelopmental disorders, as they can be reliably elicited using simple visual stimuli that are well tolerated across a wide range of developmental abilities (Köster et al., 2023).

text.text: However, studies of VEPs in idiopathic autism have reported inconsistent findings, particularly for VEP amplitudes.

Decreased N1 (N75) and/or P1 (P100) amplitudes have been reported in some studies (Kovarski et al., 2019; Siper et al., 2016), whereas others found no significant differences (Hamdan et al., 2022; Milne, 2011; Sayorwan et al., 2018; Webb et al., 2023).

text.text: Similarly, increased, decreased, or unchanged VEP amplitudes have been reported in genetic disorders associated with autism, including Phelan-McDermid syndrome (Siper et al., 2022), Rett syndrome (LeBlanc et al., 2015), fragile X syndrome (Knoth et al., 2014), and tuberous sclerosis complex (Varcin et al., 2016).

text.text: These observations suggest the need to move beyond conventional VEP amplitude measures to better understand the underlying neurophysiological mechanisms and heterogeneity of visual processing in autism.
Among studies reporting reduced VEP amplitudes in autism, at least two non-mutually exclusive, neurophysiological processes may account for this finding.
One possibility is that stimulus-evoked neural responses are intrinsically weaker, potentially reflecting reduced excitatory drive relative to inhibition (LeBlanc et al., 2015).
text.formatted: One possibility is that stimulus-evoked neural responses are intrinsically weaker, potentially reflecting reduced excitatory drive relative to inhibition <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(LeBlanc et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Another possibility is that reduced VEP amplitudes may reflect increased trial-to-trial variability in neural responses, whereby less consistent responses across repeated stimulus presentations attenuate the amplitude of the averaged VEP.
These two mechanisms may coexist and jointly contribute to the observed reduction in VEP amplitude.
This latter hypothesis has gained support from several studies employing single-trial analyses.

Using a small sample, Milne (2011) reported greater trial-to-trial variability in P1 amplitude and latency, accompanied by reduced inter-trial phase coherence, in children with autism, suggesting less consistent synchronization of stimulus-evoked neural activity. Kovarski et al. (2019) further demonstrated that the group-level P100 amplitude reduction in autism disappeared after reconstructing VEPs using only trials with consistent responses.

(2024) introduced a nonlinear mixed-effects modeling framework for trial-level VEP analysis and, using a large multisite cohort, demonstrated that children with autism exhibit significantly greater intra-individual trial-to-trial variability in P1 latency than neurotypical peers.

text.text: Beyond VEPs, studies using fMRI and steadystate visual evoked responses have also reported greater trial-to-trial neural variability and reduced response reliability in autism (Dinstein et al., 2012; Haigh et al., 2015; Weinger et al., 2014), leading to the proposal of a broader "neural unreliability" framework.

text.text: However, two important research gaps remain.

First, no study has directly quantified the relationship between trial-to-trial variability and VEP amplitude, or statistically determined whether group differences in VEP amplitude persist after accounting for such variability.
Addressing this question is important for determining whether increased trial-to-trial variability can account for reductions in VEP amplitude when they are observed in autism.
Second, no study has examined the relationship between trial-to-trial variability and developmental outcomes in children with autism.

Determining whether this neural measure is associated with cognitive or behavioral functioning is essential for evaluating its potential as a biomarker for prognosis, stratification, and treatment monitoring in autism.

Another important mechanistic question remains unanswered: what gives rise to the heightened trial-to-trial sensory variability, or "neural noise," that has been proposed to characterize autism (for a review, see Raul et al., 2024)?

text.text: One influential hypothesis is that this variability arises, at least partially, from an altered balance between neuronal excitation (E) and inhibition (I) (Rubenstein & Merzenich, 2003).

text.text: Specifically, reduced inhibitory signaling and/or excessive excitation may increase spontaneous neural activity and impair the temporal synchronization of neuronal populations required to generate consistent sensory responses (Foss-Feig et al., 2017).

text.text: In support of this hypothesis, converging evidence has implicated abnormalities in γaminobutyric acid (GABA)-mediated inhibitory signaling in autism (Robertson et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2022).

text.text: However, despite the prominence of this hypothesis, the proposed link between altered E/I balance and increased trial-to-trial neural variability has not been directly evaluated.

Although E/I balance cannot be measured non-invasively using EEG, recent advances in spectral parameterization have provided putative electrophysiological markers of cortical excitation and inhibition (Donoghue et al., 2020).

text.text: This approach decomposes the EEG power spectrum into an aperiodic 1/f component and oscillatory (periodic) activity.

Of relevance, the aperiodic exponent has been proposed as an indirect marker of E/I balance (Gao et al., 2017), whereas periodic alpha activity has been broadly associated with cortical inhibition (Chapeton et al., 2019; Klimesch et al., 2007; Mathewson et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Of relevance, the aperiodic exponent has been proposed as an indirect marker of E/I balance <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Gao et al., 2017)</ref>, whereas periodic alpha activity has been broadly associated with cortical inhibition <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Chapeton et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Klimesch et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Mathewson et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these two measures provide an opportunity to examine whether EEG features proposed to index aspects of cortical excitation and inhibition are associated with inter-trial neural variability in autism.
The present study sought to address these important questions using VEP and resting-state EEG recordings acquired from the same individuals.
The study included a large cohort of preschool-and school-aged autistic (AUT) and typically developing (TD) children.
From the VEP recordings, we quantified N1 and P1 amplitudes and inter-trial neural variability using inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC).
From resting-state EEG, we derived the aperiodic exponent and periodic alpha activity using spectral parameterization.

We first characterized group differences in these neurophysiological measures and then examined their associations with one another, as well as with developmental outcomes, including verbal and non-verbal abilities.

Together, these analyses aimed to determine whether inter-trial neural variability accounts for altered VEP amplitudes in autism and whether putative electrophysiological markers of cortical excitation and inhibition are associated with this variability.
These analyses may provide mechanistic insights into sensory processing abnormalities and their relevance to early neurodevelopment in autism.

text.text: During resting-state EEG, participants watched a screen-saver video or a preferred video for 3-5 minutes while instructed to remain quiet and still.
For the VEP paradigm, pattern-reversal black-and-white checkerboards were presented at 2 Hz on a 60-Hz monitor using E-Prime (v3, Psychology Software Tools, Inc.).
Each checkerboard square subtended a visual angle of approximately 2°.

Studies 1 and 2 continuously presented 400 and 200 trials, respectively, whereas Studies 3 and 4 used Tobii Eye-Tracking to present 200 and 100 gaze-dependent trials, respectively, when participants were looking at the screen.
EEG was recorded in a dimly lit, sound-attenuated, electrically shielded room.
Participants sat independently or on a caregiver's lap, with caregivers instructed not to speak or socially engage with the child during recording.
EEG data were acquired using a 128-channel HydroCel Geodesic Sensor Net (Version 1, EGI Inc., Eugene, OR) connected to a DC-coupled amplifier (Net Amps 400, EGI Inc., Eugene, OR).
In Studies 1-3, electrode impedances were maintained below 50 kΩ, and data were sampled at 1,000 Hz.
In Study 4, electrode impedances were maintained below 100 kΩ, and the sampling rate was set at 500 Hz.
All studies used Cz as the reference electrode.
Following acquisition, session videos were reviewed using AVOCODO (Audio/VideO CODing Optimization) (An, 2026), a MATLAB-based behavioral coding tool.

text.text: We recorded visual evoked potentials (VEPs) and resting EEG from children aged 2-12 years with and without autism.
We compared VEP component amplitudes across groups and found significantly reduced N1 and marginally reduced N1-P1 amplitudes in the autism (AUT) group.
These VEP differences were significantly associated with, and largely explained by, the intertrial phase coherence (ITPC), a measure of trial-to-trial variability in visual stimulus processing.

Moreover, ITPC was positively correlated with the aperiodic exponent and periodic alpha activity in resting EEG, suggesting a potential mechanistic link between greater visual processing variability and reduced network inhibition and/or excitation-inhibition imbalance.

Finally, within the autism group, higher nonverbal cognitive and language abilities were significantly associated with greater ITPC, indicating that visual processing consistency may play an important functional role in early cognitive development and learning.
Using a large cohort of children, we demonstrated decreased N1 and marginally decreased N1-P1 amplitudes in autism.

These findings are broadly consistent with prior studies on children with idiopathic autism (Kovarski et al., 2019; Siper et al., 2016) as well as in some autismassociated neurodevelopmental disorders such as Rett syndrome (LeBlanc et al., 2015; Saby et al., 2023) and Phelan-McDermid syndrome (Siper et al., 2022).

text.text: Conversely, other autismassociated disorders, such as fragile X syndrome, have reported a higher N1 amplitude compared to controls (Knoth et al., 2014), suggesting that distinct neurobiological mechanisms may underlie sensory processing abnormalities across these genetically defined disorders.

text.text: Importantly, we provide direct evidence that these conventional VEP amplitude differences are closely related to trial-to-trial phase consistency, as indexed by inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC), and may not reflect intrinsically weaker single-trial responses.

Specifically, autistic children exhibited significantly lower stimulus-evoked phase synchrony than typically developing peers, indicating less consistent neural responses across repeated presentations of identical visual stimuli.

Furthermore, the group differences in N1 and N1-P1 amplitudes were no longer significant after accounting for ITPC, suggesting that increased inter-trial variability provides a more compelling explanation for the observed VEP amplitude reductions than intrinsically weaker stimulus-evoked neural responses.

Together, these findings are consistent with previous reports of increased inter-trial variability in autistic children (Kovarski et al., 2019; Milne, 2011) and provide direct quantitative support for this proposed mechanism.

text.text: To our knowledge, this study is the first to report a significant cross-sectional age-related increase in ITPC in both autistic and typically developing children.

Although our cross-sectional data do not allow us to conclude that inter-trial variability decreases within individuals over development, they raise important questions regarding the developmental trajectory of neural response consistency in autism.

Sensory experience is known to continuously refine cortical circuits through experience-dependent plasticity, leading to progressively more specialized and efficient sensory processing over development (for review, see Ribic, 2020).

text.text: Although this process has not been explicitly examined in relation to inter-trial variability in autism, it is possible that experience-dependent refinement also shapes sensory development in autistic individuals, albeit potentially through altered or delayed developmental pathways (Beker et al., 2018; Robertson & Baron-Cohen, 2017).

text.text: Within this framework, the observed age-related increase in ITPC may reflect progressively more synchronized and reliable neural responses to repeated visual stimulation as cortical circuits mature.

Longitudinal studies are needed to determine whether neural response consistency increases within individuals across development and whether this developmental trajectory differs between autistic and typically developing children.
More pronounced periodic alpha activity and a steeper aperiodic exponent during resting-state EEG were both associated with greater ITPC and larger VEP amplitudes.

Alpha oscillations have long been associated with cortical inhibition and attentional gating (Chapeton et al., 2019; Klimesch et al., 2007; Mathewson et al., 2011), whereas the aperiodic exponent has been proposed to reflect the balance between cortical excitation and inhibition (E/I), with steeper exponents indicating relatively greater inhibitory tone (Gao et al., 2017; Waschke et al., 2021).

text.text: Together, these findings suggest that stronger cortical inhibition is associated with more reliable stimulus-evoked neural responses, and provide support for the hypothesis that altered E/I balance contributes to increased neural variability, or "neural noise," in autism (Raul et al., 2024; Rubenstein & Merzenich, 2003).

text.text: While previous studies have proposed this relationship conceptually, our findings quantitatively link putative resting-state markers of cortical inhibition to the consistency of sensory-evoked neural responses.
One plausible mechanism is that inhibitory circuits stabilize the recruitment of neuronal populations during sensory processing (Isaacson & Scanziani, 2011).
text.formatted: One plausible mechanism is that inhibitory circuits stabilize the recruitment of neuronal populations during sensory processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Isaacson & Scanziani, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: GABAergic inhibition sharpens stimulus selectivity and suppresses competing neural responses, thereby promoting consistent activation of similar neuronal populations across repeated presentations of the same stimulus.

Conversely, when inhibitory control is reduced, cortical activity becomes more susceptible to ongoing spontaneous activations, such that identical sensory inputs may recruit partially different neuronal populations or engage them with less precise temporal coordination across trials.
This would manifest as reduced phase consistency (lower ITPC) and, consequently, smaller averaged VEP amplitudes due to greater cancellation during trial averaging.

This interpretation is consistent with evidence of altered GABAergic signaling in autism (Robertson et al., 2016) and theoretical models proposing that reduced inhibition destabilizes cortical computations and increases intrinsic neural noise.

text.text: Several considerations should be noted when interpreting these findings.
First, our results should not be interpreted as suggesting that greater inhibition or lower neural noise is invariably beneficial.

According to the High Noise-Stochastic Resonance (HNSR) framework (Raul et al., 2024), an intermediate level of intrinsic neural noise may enhance the detection of weak sensory inputs, whereas excessive noise compromises the fidelity and reliability of sensory representations.
text.formatted: According to the High Noise-Stochastic Resonance (HNSR) framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Raul et al., 2024)</ref>, an intermediate level of intrinsic neural noise may enhance the detection of weak sensory inputs, whereas excessive noise compromises the fidelity and reliability of sensory representations.

text.text: Therefore, our findings are more consistent with the notion that elevated neural variability becomes maladaptive when it exceeds an optimal range, rather than implying that neural noise should be minimized.
Second, we do not propose altered E/I balance to be the sole contributor to the elevated visual processing variability observed in autism.
Indeed, the associations between resting EEG measures and ITPC were only moderate, indicating that substantial variance remains unexplained.

Other factors, including ongoing fluctuations in cortical state, attention, neuromodulatory processes, and large-scale network organization, may also influence the consistency of sensory processing across repeated stimulus presentations.

Our exploratory analyses further suggested that higher ITPC, reflecting greater consistency in visual processing, was associated with better nonverbal cognition, verbal comprehension, and language abilities.
Although derived from a visual paradigm, this finding may reflect a broader property of cortical sensory processing rather than a modality-specific phenomenon.

Reliable sensory representations provide a critical foundation for early brain development, as experience-dependent plasticity relies on repeated and consistent sensory inputs to refine cortical circuits, strengthen relevant synaptic connections, and establish efficient neural representations (Hensch, 2005; Ribic, 2020).

text.text: Such reliable sensory encoding is particularly important during early childhood, when the acquisition of higher-order cognitive functions, including language, depends on accurate and consistent sensory feedback from the environment (Kuhl, 2004 (Kuhl, , 2010;; Werker & Hensch, 2015).

text.text: Within this framework, increased trialto-trial variability may reduce the fidelity of sensory representations available for learning, thereby limiting the efficiency with which sensory experiences are translated into cognitive and language development.

Although these cross-sectional associations cannot establish causality, they suggest that sensory response consistency may serve as a concurrent marker of developmental functioning in autism and motivate future longitudinal studies to determine whether early neural variability predicts later developmental outcomes.

A recent study of infants with a high familial likelihood for autism reported that greater trial-totrial variability in VEPs during the first year of life predicted better language and cognitive outcomes at 24 months (Dickinson et al., 2026).

text.text: These seemingly contradictory findings, however, may instead provide important insight into the changing role of neural variability across development.
During infancy, the cortex undergoes rapid expansion of excitatory synaptic connections and exhibits exceptionally high levels of experience-dependent plasticity.
Greater neural variability during this period may therefore reflect a more dynamic and adaptable cortical system that facilitates circuit refinement and learning.

As development progresses, however, maturation of inhibitory circuitry together with activity-dependent synaptic pruning gradually stabilizes cortical networks, increasing the fidelity and reliability of sensory representations (Hensch, 2005).
text.formatted: As development progresses, however, maturation of inhibitory circuitry together with activity-dependent synaptic pruning gradually stabilizes cortical networks, increasing the fidelity and reliability of sensory representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hensch, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Within this developmental framework, greater neural variability may be advantageous during infancy by promoting plasticity, whereas lower variability during the preschool and school years may instead reflect more mature and efficient sensory processing.

Together, these findings suggest that the functional significance of neural variability is developmentally dependent, with different levels of variability supporting optimal brain function at different stages of neurodevelopment.
Several limitations of this study should be acknowledged.

First, the cross-sectional design precludes direct characterization of within-individual developmental changes or causal relationships among cortical inhibition, neural variability, and developmental outcomes.
Longitudinal studies spanning infancy through childhood will be important for delineating the developmental trajectories of these neurophysiological measures.
Second, consistent with the higher prevalence of autism in males, our cohort was predominantly male, which limited our ability to examine potential sex differences in these neural measures.
Finally, developmental assessments were available for only a subset of participants, and when available, cognitive testing was not always conducted concurrently with EEG acquisition.
These factors likely reduced statistical power and may have attenuated the observed brain-behavior associations.

Future studies with more comprehensive and temporally aligned phenotyping will be important for further establishing the relationship between neural response consistency and developmental functioning.

In a large cohort of autistic and typically developing children, we demonstrate that reduced VEP amplitudes in autism are closely related to increased trial-to-trial variability in visual neural responses.

Group differences in VEP amplitudes were no longer significant after accounting for ITPC, suggesting that conventional averaged VEP measures may partly reflect the consistency, rather than simply the strength, of underlying stimulus-evoked responses.

Furthermore, associations between ITPC and resting-state periodic alpha activity and aperiodic exponent provide support for a potential contribution of cortical excitation/inhibition to sensory response reliability.
Finally, the association between greater ITPC and better cognitive and language abilities in autistic children highlights the potential developmental relevance of neural response consistency.
Together, these findings position trial-to-trial neural variability as an important dimension of sensory processing in autism.
